Joel — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

The prophet Joel warned of destruction coming upon Judah through locusts and other insects.

He called the people to repentance, fasting and prayer.

He also spoke of the blessings of the gospel and the final glorious state of the church.

The devastating plague of locusts (verses 1–7)

Even the oldest people could not remember a disaster like the one about to strike Judah.

Swarms of insects would consume the crops and fruit of the land.

Henry says the language can also describe destruction by a foreign invading army.

He sees a possible reference to the devastation caused by the Chaldeans.

God is the Lord of hosts.

Every created thing obeys his command.

When he chooses, he can humble a proud and rebellious people through the smallest and most despised creatures.

God is just to remove comforts that people misuse through luxury and excess.

The more we place our happiness in bodily pleasure, the more painful it is when outward blessings are taken away.

Every extra earthly comfort we treat as necessary for happiness increases our vulnerability to loss.

Everyone is called to mourn (verses 8–13)

Those who labor only for food that perishes will eventually find that their efforts bring disappointment.

People whose joy depends upon bodily pleasures lose that joy as soon as the pleasures are interrupted or removed.

Spiritual joy, however, can flourish precisely when outward comforts fail.

Notice how uncertain and temporary created comforts are.

We need to live in constant dependence upon God and his providential care.

Notice too the destruction produced by sin.

When poverty causes true worship and godliness to weaken and deprives people of spiritual instruction, the judgment is especially severe.

Yet God's judgments can also be merciful awakenings, stirring his people from sleep and drawing their hearts back to Christ and his salvation.

The people must turn to God (verses 14–20)

The sorrow of the people was to become repentance and humility before God.

Alongside signs of grief and shame, they were to confess and mourn their sins.

A day was to be set apart for this purpose.

People would leave ordinary work to give more attention to God's worship and abstain from food and drink as they fasted.

Everyone had contributed to the nation's guilt, and everyone shared in its calamity.

Therefore everyone was called to join in repentance.

When joy disappears from God's house, sincere religion declines and love grows cold, it is time to cry out to the Lord.

The prophet described the severity of the disaster.

Even animals suffered because of human wrongdoing.

Those who cry to God only because they want food and drink, without concern for their sin, behave little better than animals.

Yet even an animal's cries for food shame the hardness of people who never cry to God for anything.

Whatever becomes of nations or churches that persist in wickedness, believers will still find comfort in being accepted by God, when the unrepentant face his judgment.
classic_reading:
[Joel.1.1-Joel.1.7]
Joel
From the desolations about to come upon the land of Judah, by the ravages of locusts and other insects, the prophet Joel exhorts the Jews to repentance, fasting, and prayer. He notices the blessings of the gospel, with the final glorious state of the church.
Chapter 1
A plague of locusts. (Joel 1:1-7) All sorts of people are called to lament it. (Joel 1:8-13) They are to look to God. (Joel 1:14-20)
Verses 1-7 The most aged could not remember such calamities as were about to take place. Armies of insects were coming upon the land to eat the fruits of it. It is expressed so as to apply also to the destruction of the country by a foreign enemy, and seems to refer to the devastations of the Chaldeans. God is Lord of hosts, has every creature at his command, and, when he pleases, can humble and mortify a proud, rebellious people, by the weakest and most contemptible creatures. It is just with God to take away the comforts which are abused to luxury and excess; and the more men place their happiness in the gratifications of sense, the more severe temporal afflictions are upon them. The more earthly delights we make needful to satisfy us, the more we expose ourselves to trouble.
[Joel.1.8-Joel.1.13]
Verses 8-13 All who labour only for the meat that perishes, will, sooner or later, be ashamed of their labour. Those that place their happiness in the delights of sense, when deprived of them, or disturbed in the enjoyment, lose their joy; whereas spiritual joy then flourishes more than ever. See what perishing, uncertain things our creature-comforts are. See how we need to live in continual dependence upon God and his providence. See what ruinous work sin makes. As far as poverty occasions the decay of piety, and starves the cause of religion among a people, it is a very sore judgment. But how blessed are the awakening judgments of God, in rousing his people and calling home the heart to Christ, and his salvation!
[Joel.1.14-Joel.1.20]
Verses 14-20 The sorrow of the people is turned into repentance and humiliation before God. With all the marks of sorrow and shame, sin must be confessed and bewailed. A day is to be appointed for this purpose; a day in which people must be kept from their common employments, that they may more closely attend God's services; and there is to be abstaining from meat and drink. Every one had added to the national guilt, all shared in the national calamity, therefore every one must join in repentance. When joy and gladness are cut off from God's house, when serious godliness decays, and love waxes cold, then it is time to cry unto the Lord. The prophet describes how grievous the calamity. See even the inferior creatures suffering for our transgression. And what better are they than beasts, who never cry to God but for corn and wine, and complain of the want of the delights of sense? Yet their crying to God in those cases, shames the stupidity of those who cry not to God in any case. Whatever may become of the nations and churches that persist in ungodliness, believers will find the comfort of acceptance with God, when the wicked shall be burned up with his indignation.

The coming judgment and call to repentance (verses 1–14)

The priests were commanded to sound the alarm about God's approaching judgments.

God's ministers must warn people about the terrible consequences of sin and reveal his judgment against human ungodliness and unrighteousness.

The vivid description portrays the devastation caused by locusts.

Henry says it may also describe the destruction wrought by Chaldean invaders.

If sinful nations need warnings about earthly disasters, how much more urgently must sinners seek rescue from the wrath to come!

Our chief concern in this life should be belonging to our Lord Jesus Christ.

We should loosen our attachment to things that will soon be taken from everyone who treats them as idols.

Repentance includes outward signs of sorrow and shame—fasting, weeping and mourning.

But tears over hardship should become tears over the sin that caused it.

Tearing our clothes is worthless if our hearts remain unbroken.

True repentance requires humbling ourselves, mourning our wrongdoing and turning away from it.

Henry says we may be confident that God will forgive genuine repentance.

But he distinguishes this from the removal of every outward affliction: that is not promised, though the possibility of relief encourages us to turn back.

A public fast and the promise of mercy (verses 15–27)

The priests and rulers were called to proclaim a solemn fast.

The sinner's plea is simple: “Spare us, good Lord.”

God is ready to help his people.

He waits to show grace.

The people asked for mercy, and he answered their prayer.

His promises are genuine answers to prayers offered in faith.

With God, speaking and acting are not separate matters.

Henry notes that some interpreters understand these promises figuratively.

On that reading, they point toward the grace of the gospel and are fulfilled through the abundant comforts kept for believers in the covenant of grace.

The Holy Spirit is promised (verses 28–32)

The promise began to be fulfilled at Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit was poured out.

It continued through converting grace and miraculous gifts, given to both Jews and Gentiles.

God's judgments upon a sinful world precede the final judgment of the world.

To call on the Lord truly involves knowing him, having faith in him, desiring him and depending upon him.

It must also be accompanied by conscientious obedience, which demonstrates that this faith is sincere.

Those who will be delivered on the great and final day are the people effectively called from sin to God, from self to Christ, and from earthly things to heavenly things.
classic_reading:
[Joel.2.1-Joel.2.14]
Chapter 2
God's judgments. (Joel 2:1-14) Exhortations to fasting and prayer; blessings promised. (Joel 2:15-27) A promise of the Holy Spirit, and of future mercies. (Joel 2:28-32)
Verses 1-14 The priests were to alarm the people with the near approach of the Divine judgments. It is the work of ministers to warn of the fatal consequences of sin, and to reveal the wrath from heaven against the ungodliness and unrighteousness of men. The striking description which follows, shows what would attend the devastations of locusts, but may also describe the effects from the ravaging of the land by the Chaldeans. If the alarm of temporal judgments is given to offending nations, how much more should sinners be warned to seek deliverance from the wrath to come! Our business therefore on earth must especially be, to secure an interest in our Lord Jesus Christ; and we should seek to be weaned from objects which will soon be torn from all who now make idols of them. There must be outward expressions of sorrow and shame, fasting, weeping, and mourning; tears for trouble must be turned into tears for the sin that caused it. But rending the garments would be vain, except their hearts were rent by abasement and self-abhorrence; by sorrow for their sins, and separation from them. There is no question but that if we truly repent of our sins, God will forgive them; but whether he will remove affliction is not promised, yet the probability of it should encourage us to repent.
[Joel.2.15-Joel.2.27]
Verses 15-27 The priests and rulers are to appoint a solemn fast. The sinner's supplication is, Spare us, good Lord. God is ready to succour his people; and he waits to be gracious. They prayed that God would spare them, and he answered them. His promises are real answers to the prayers of faith; with him saying and doing are not two things. Some understand these promises figuratively, as pointing to gospel grace, and as fulfilled in the abundant comforts treasured up for believers in the covenant of grace.
[Joel.2.28-Joel.2.32]
Verses 28-32 The promise began to be fulfilled on the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit was poured out, and it was continued in the converting grace and miraculous gifts conferred on both Jews and Gentiles. The judgments of God upon a sinful world, only go before the judgment of the world in the last day. Calling on God supposes knowledge of him, faith in him, desire toward him, dependence on him, and, as evidence of the sincerity of all this, conscientious obedience to him. Those only shall be delivered in the great day, who are now effectually called from sin to God, from self to Christ, from things below to things above.

Judgment upon the nations (verses 1–8)

Henry understands this passage as foretelling the restoration of the Jews and the final victory of true religion over its enemies.

It recalls the contempt with which Jewish people have often been treated and the low value placed upon their lives.

No one has hardened the heart against God or his church and enjoyed lasting prosperity.

The day of judgment (verses 9–17)

The prophecy challenges all who oppose God's people.

There will be no escape from divine judgment.

In that day, unrepentant sinners will be cut off from every source of comfort and joy.

Henry notes that many prophets predict the final victory of God's church over those who oppose it.

The same day will be terrible for the wicked but joyful for the righteous.

Those who belong to Christ have reason to rejoice in their Strength and Redeemer.

The acceptable year of the Lord, so full of mercy for some, will be a day of extraordinary judgment for others.

Everyone who remains apart from Christ should awaken and flee from the wrath to come.

The church's future blessings (verses 18–21)

God will pour out his blessings abundantly, and the gospel will spread swiftly to the farthest regions of the earth.

The prophet speaks through meaningful symbols.

A day is coming when everything wrong will finally be made right.

The source of these abundant blessings is God's own house, from which the streams flow.

Christ is that Fountain.

His suffering, merit and grace cleanse, refresh and make people spiritually fruitful.

The grace of the gospel flowing from Christ will reach the Gentile world, even the most distant lands.

It will produce the fruits of righteousness among them.

All the good we enjoy now—and all we hope to enjoy forever—flows from the Lord's house above, his heavenly temple.
classic_reading:
[Joel.3.1-Joel.3.8]
Chapter 3
God's judgments in the latter days. (Joel 3:1-8) The extent of these judgments. (Joel 3:9-17) The blessings the church shall enjoy. (Joel 3:18-21)
Verses 1-8 The restoration of the Jews, and the final victory of true religion over all opposers, appear to be here foretold. The contempt and scorn with which the Jews have often been treated as a people, and the little value set upon them, are noticed. None ever hardened his heart against God or his church, and prospered long.
[Joel.3.9-Joel.3.17]
Verses 9-17 Here is a challenge to all the enemies of God's people. There is no escaping God's judgments; hardened sinners, in that day of wrath, shall be cut off from all comfort and joy. Most of the prophets foretell the same final victory of the church of God over all that oppose it. To the wicked it will be a terrible day, but to the righteous it will be a joyful day. What cause have those who possess an interest in Christ, to glory in their Strength and their Redeemer! The acceptable year of the Lord, a day of such great favour to some, will be a day of remarkable vengeance to others: let every one that is out of Christ awake, and flee from the wrath to come.
[Joel.3.18-Joel.3.21]
Verses 18-21 There shall be abundant Divine influences, and the gospel will spread speedily into the remotest corners of the earth. These events are predicted under significant emblems; there is a day coming, when every thing amiss shall be amended. The fountain of this plenty is in the house of God, whence the streams take rise. Christ is this Fountain; his sufferings, merit, and grace, cleanse, refresh, and make fruitful. Gospel grace, flowing from Christ, shall reach to the Gentile world, to the most remote regions, and make them abound in fruits of righteousness; and from the house of the Lord above, from his heavenly temple, flows all the good we daily taste, and hope to enjoy eternally.
